annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygon features mark identifiable housing association property parcels/buildings, not a tessellated reporting zone. The decisive rule is object: these are bounded real-world properties with ownership/house counts.
Point features mark individual archaeological cesspits/finds at specific addresses, so the geometry is PointDS and the main entity is identifiable real-world objects rather than amounts or events.
The layer is a point FeatureCollection of archaeological finds/locations. Each point marks a distinct object or find spot (object codes, photos, descriptions), so PointDS + ObjectDS fits best.
Polygon features mark individual archaeological sites/vindplaatsen with names, addresses, and descriptions; they are selected bounded objects, not a tessellation or full-area coverage.
Polygon regions mark named parks and green spaces with BBQ rules; these are identifiable bounded objects, not a tessellated reporting layer or full-area coverage.

Polygon areas are named protected city/district conservation zones, not a full tessellation or reporting lattice. Main meaning is identifiable bounded heritage areas, so ObjectDS with PlainVectorRegion.
Point features represent bee observation locations; each point is a distinct real-world observed place/object, not a network, amount, or event layer.
Point features represent honey bee locations/apiaries, and the decisive attribute is numeric quantity (Aantal_volken / Aantal_kasten), so this is a point-based amount layer.
Polygon layer classifying Amsterdam soil quality into zone categories (e.g., Zone 1–7, saneringsgebied) across the study area, so it is a tessellated full-area thematic coverage.
Point geometry with 70,000 individually identified trees (tree number, species, height, owner/manager) indicates distinct real-world objects, not measures or events.
Point features representing individual trees; each point is a distinct real-world object, so PointDS + ObjectDS.
Point features represent individual trees (distinct, countable real-world objects), so Geometry is PointDS and Entity is ObjectDS.
Point features represent individual trees identified by tree number and species, so this is a point object layer (not network, event, or amount).
Point features marking individual neighborhood compost locations; each point is a distinct real-world facility/object, not a measurement or event.
Polygon areas named as camera areas; they are selected bounded regions, not a full tessellation. By the object/area rule, these named bounded zones are best classified as ObjectDS.
Point locations for individual trees; each feature is a distinct real-world object (a Canadian poplar), not a measurement or event. Classified by point geometry + object rule.
Point features representing identifiable crowd-monitoring sensors/cameras; not a network or measure. Decisive rule: point geometry + real-world objects.
Polygon areas represent selected cultural-historical exploration zones, not a full tessellation or reporting units; best fits bounded area patches.
Point features mark knotweed occurrences/patches, not a reporting or full-coverage layer; the decisive rule is bounded phenomenon patch at point locations.
Point features marking ecopassage problem/solution locations; main meaning is identifiable real-world objects/locations rather than measurements or events.

Polygon areas mark selected potential wind-energy sites, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is patch-like bounded zones with numeric attributes for capacity/output, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Point geometry with 744 voting-location features; each point is a distinct real-world stemlocatie (polling place), so this is best classified as ObjectDS rather than measures or events.

Point layer marking individual trees/brood nests tied to Boom_IDs; each point is a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event. The decisive rule is point geometry with object-like entities.
Polygon layer of pedicab areas that partitions the city into allowed/forbidden zones; this is a full-area thematic classification, so VectorTessellation + CoverageDS.
Point features mark specific pedicab/coach stand locations; the decisive rule is point geometry + identifiable real-world objects/facilities, not amounts or events.
Point features each mark a distinct non-residential object/building with address and function attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Polygon layer of block/street units classified by function-mix percentages (WON/VZN/WRK); this is a tessellation and the main meaning is a full-area thematic coverage classification.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam; the decisive rule is tessellation. The layer is a reporting/administrative unit layer (buurtcombinaties) with codes and area, so LatticeDS fits.
Neighborhood polygons covering Amsterdam’s area (excl. water) form a near-complete partition, and the attributes identify reporting units with codes and area; this matches tessellation + lattice.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so the geometry is a tessellation. They are reporting/statistical units with codes and area attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, and the layer is a reporting/statistical unit map (buurten) with codes and area attributes, so tessellation + lattice.
City districts are administrative reporting units that partition Amsterdam, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is a lattice (district units with attached attributes like area).
City districts are administrative reporting units that partition Amsterdam; the polygons form a tessellation, so this is a lattice/reporting-unit layer.

Polygon layer of 22 named Amsterdam areas that functions as a complete area partition; decisive rules are tessellation and reporting-unit style area division (Gebied/Stadsdeel codes with area attributes).
Polygon areas named by Amsterdam districts/areas with codes and area fields; they form a near-complete area division, so this is a tessellation of reporting units (gebiedsindeling).

Polygon areas named as practice areas and tied to stadsdeel codes indicate a partition of Amsterdam into reporting/administrative units; this matches tessellation and the reporting-unit (lattice) rule.
Polygons represent Amsterdam practice areas that subdivide the city into reporting units, with area attributes; this fits tessellation + lattice.
Polygon regions represent industrial noise contour zones (50 dB etc.); this is an isoline/interval-style contour layer, not a tessellation or reporting unit layer.
Polygon bands represent noise contour intervals (55-60, 60-65, 65-70, >70 dB), so this is a contour/interval map; the regions do not form a reporting tessellation, so Geometry is PlainVectorRegion.
Polygon features form contour bands for traffic noise levels (dB classes), so the layer is a tessellated contour map rather than isolated patches or reporting units.
Polygon regions form a contour-style tessellation of noise bands (e.g., 50-55 dB, 55-60 dB), so the geometry is VectorTessellation and the entity is ContourDS.
Point features represent voting locations (Stembureau/Stemlocatie), and the main meaning is numeric election results and turnout counts/percentages, so PointDS + AmountDS.
Point features marking individual green roof locations by address; the layer is about identifiable real-world objects (green roofs), not a network or measurement field.
Land use 2017 is an area-wide thematic classification of polygon classes that together partition the city; this matches tessellation geometry and coverage entity.
Point geometries mark individual historical buildings/structures (e.g., churches, gates, monasteries), so this is a set of identifiable real-world objects rather than measurements or events.

The layer uses polygons for municipality areas, which are reporting/administrative units rather than isolated patches. By the tessellation and reporting-unit rules, Geometry is VectorTessellation and Entity is LatticeDS.

Polygons form a citywide set of dog-rule areas, and the layer classifies area-wide restrictions/permissions rather than reporting units or individual objects; this matches a tessellation-style coverage map.

Polygon regions are individual named green areas in Amsterdam’s Main Green Structure, not a full tessellation; the decisive rule is object-like bounded areas (parks, cemeteries, corridors) rather than reporting units or coverage.
Point features represent individual elm trees ('Iepen particulier'); this is a set of identifiable real-world objects, not amounts or events.
Point features mark housing locations, and the key attribute is Aantal_woningen (number of dwellings), so the decisive rule is point data with numeric magnitude = AmountDS.
Point features mark individual chestnut trees; the layer is about identifiable real-world objects, not counts or coverage. The decisive rule is point geometry -> ObjectDS.
Point features with numeric fields for ground level and groundwater depth; the layer is a sampled measurement of a continuous phenomenon at locations, so PointDS + PointMeasuresDS.
Polygon layer of flood risk classes (chance/depth) covering the area as a thematic classification, so it fits tessellation geometry and full-area coverage.
Point geometry with named market locations; each point is a distinct real-world market object/place, so ObjectDS fits best.
Point geometry with named, countable green monuments/park objects; not a network or amount. Each point denotes a distinct real-world monument object.
Point features mark individual monumental trees, which are distinct real-world objects rather than measurements or events.
Point geometry with each point representing a distinct monument/object (monument status, name, address). Decisive rule: identifiable real-world objects.
Point geometry with 1530 plant observations; each point marks a distinct quay-wall plant record/species occurrence rather than a measure or event, so ObjectDS fits best.

Polygon layer of 3292 areas keyed by code/year, representing NO2 measurement values over time. The polygons act as a tessellation/reporting-unit layer, and the main meaning is a numeric magnitude (NO2 concentration), so AmountDS.
Point geometry with 302 named NO2 measurement locations; decisive rule is point locations representing distinct monitoring sites/objects rather than a field or event.
Polygon features do not form a full tessellation; the layer is a bounded area map of primeval gulch zones. The decisive rule is patch/selected area rather than reporting unit or coverage.
Point soundings/boreholes are sampled measurement locations, and the key attributes are depth/elevation values (e.g., Top_Pleistoceen), so this is PointDS with PointMeasuresDS.

Polygon regions that are named development neighbourhoods, not a full tessellation for statistical reporting. Best fit is object-like bounded areas (development neighbourhoods) rather than coverage or lattice.
Point features mark individual public toilet locations; the decisive rule is distinct real-world objects represented by points.

Polygon features are neighbourhood/area units that partition Amsterdam, so Geometry is tessellation. The layer marks where overnight/hotel policy is allowed or not allowed by area (SELECTIE TENZIJ/NIET), so the main meaning is Boolean presence/permission status, fitting ExistenceDS.
Polygon layer of parking standards categories; the regions are a tessellated area-wide thematic classification, so use VectorTessellation and CoverageDS.

Polygon/multipolygon features represent named parks and green spaces, not a full tessellation. The decisive rule is object: each polygon is an identifiable park or public green asset, with area as an attribute.

Polygons are postcode areas that partition the city, so geometry is a tessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units: postcode4 zones are aggregation units with area attributes (Opp_m2).

Polygon postcode areas form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam, so geometry is tessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units: postcode4 areas with area attribute, so LatticeDS.
Polygon postcode6 areas intended as a complete territorial partition; the decisive rule is reporting/statistical units, so this is a lattice.

LineString road/transport infrastructure layer; the decisive rule is network-like line features, but the allowed entity set lacks NetworkDS, so these are best treated as identifiable linear objects (roads/networks) rather than areas or counts.

Polygons are selected pedestrian-area regions rather than a complete tessellation. The key attribute is a categorical area-wide classification (plein_park: Park/Plein), so this is a coverage-style thematic layer.
Point features with named locations (e.g., bridges, sluices, buildings) indicate distinct real-world objects; the decisive rule is point geometry plus object-like place names.
Point geometry with each point marking a distinct privacy-related investigation/type entry; treated as identifiable objects rather than measurements, events, or amounts.

Point features mark specific scan locations along streets; the decisive rule is point geometry with each point representing a distinct real-world location/object rather than an amount, event, or network.
Point features mark voting locations/precinct results, and the main meaning is numeric election counts and percentages (amounts) rather than objects or events.

Polygon regions mark drainage feasibility zones, not a full tessellation or reporting grid; the decisive rule is Boolean presence/absence of drainage possibility (Mogelijk/Niet mogelijk), so ExistenceDS.
Polygons are selected hydro unit areas, not a full tessellation of Amsterdam. The layer is about Rainproof solution areas/units by ID, so the decisive rule is bounded selected regions -> PatchDS.
Polygon areas mark specific rainproof bottleneck zones with descriptions of local water accumulation; they are selected problem areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units, so PatchDS.
Polygon features are selected locations rather than a tessellation; the layer names specific polder sewerage sites/objects (Locatie), so ObjectDS is the best fit.
Point features mark distinct religious buildings/places (churches, mosques, temples), so the layer is best read as identifiable objects rather than measures or events.

Line geometries represent sidewalk segments, and the main attribute is sidewalk width (a numeric magnitude) with obstacle/space-claim counts. This fits a line-based AmountDS rather than a network-routing layer.
Line geometry with named street segments and road-side directions; this is a set of identifiable linear road-related objects, not a network flow layer.
Point features for public playground/sport facilities; each point is a distinct real-world object/facility, so use ObjectDS.
Point locations of city farming sites with names/addresses; each point is a distinct real-world place/facility, so PointDS + ObjectDS.

Polygon features are individual named city farming sites, not a full tessellation. The decisive rule is object: each bounded area is a distinct real-world facility/park, so ObjectDS fits better than patch or coverage.
Point geometry with named initiatives/activities and years; the decisive rule is point-based identifiable objects/places rather than measures or events.
LineString features define a line layer, and the decisive rule is major street features: connected road objects rather than a network flow or numeric measure.

Line geometry and the title/attributes indicate district heating/cooling transport infrastructure; by the network rule this is a transport/utility line system, with status categories as supporting attributes.

Polygon areas mark district heating/cooling zones with construction/operation status; they are selected bounded service areas, not a reporting tessellation or full-area coverage, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Polygon project areas for housing plans; not a full tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion. Main meaning is numeric housing capacity (Aantal_woningen_max), so AmountDS.
Point features marking named local farming product businesses/places; classification follows point geometry and identifiable real-world objects (not amounts, events, or network).
LineString features represent tram and metro routes, so geometry is LineDS. By the network/route-system rule, the main phenomenon is connected transport lines rather than objects or areas.

LineString geometry and the layer title indicate tram and metro lines; this is a connected transport network, but among the allowed entity labels the best fit is ObjectDS for distinct linear features.
Point geometry and the layer is a list of tram stops and metro stations, so the decisive rule is object points representing real-world transit facilities.
Point geometry with named tram stops and metro stations; each point is a distinct transit facility/object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual traffic light intersections/objects; not a network, amount, or event. Decisive rule: point geometry with identifiable real-world objects.
Line geometries represent road links in a traffic prognosis network, and the attributes are numeric traffic volumes by time period; network/amount rules apply.
Point features mark election polling places, and the main meaning is numeric vote/turnout magnitude at each location (amount-based election results).
Point features mark individual trees with ID, species, planting year, and size classes; this is a set of identifiable real-world objects, not a network or amount.
Point features representing identifiable traffic information system devices (e.g., cameras, displays, sensors); this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features marking individual traffic information system installations (BFA devices); decisive rule is identifiable real-world objects at point locations.
Point features mark bird nesting locations, and the main meaning is numeric magnitude via per-year counts (Aantal_2011–2020), so this is PointDS with AmountDS.
Point features mark individual benches in Vondelpark; the decisive rule is identifiable real-world object, not measurement or event.

LineString street segments indicate LineDS. The layer rates walkability and crowding with ordinal magnitude categories (e.g., goed, matig, druk), so the main meaning is an amount/intensity classification rather than objects or events.
Point geometry with 226 distinct wall-art artworks at building addresses; each feature is an identifiable real-world object, so ObjectDS fits best.
Polygon layer of area-wide welstandniveaus; the regions form a thematic classification over the study area, so this is a tessellation with coverage semantics.
Polygon layer of building/urban style systems that categorizes the whole area into thematic classes; this fits a near-complete tessellation and a full-area coverage classification.
Point features mark WWII attack/incidents at addresses; the decisive rule is point geometry with event-based meaning (something that happened at a place and date).

Polygon areas represent individual housing project/planning zones, not a full tessellation or reporting grid. Main meaning is bounded development plan patches with housing counts as attributes, so PatchDS fits best.
Point features mark individual self-build plot projects/locations; the layer is about identifiable real-world objects (project sites), not measurements or events.

Polygon layer uses a near-area-wide categorical classification by Categorie (historical/attention classes), so the decisive rule is full-area thematic classification -> CoverageDS; polygons function as a tessellation of mapped areas.
Point features represent solar panel locations; attributes are numeric counts and capacity (gedetecteerde_panelen, vermogen), so the decisive rule is point data with main meaning as amount.
Point features mark named swimming locations and facilities (e.g., beaches, pools), so the layer is best treated as identifiable objects rather than measures or events.
